meta.blurb: A small, shabby priest with a round face and an umbrella understands crime better than any detective. In six famous tales, Father Brown outwits the master thief Flambeau, solves an impossible murder and uncovers a hero's dark secret.
meta.bible: Father Brown: a small, round-faced Catholic priest from Essex, shabby and mild, with a large umbrella; he has heard so many confessions that he understands how evil thinks. Flambeau: a huge, clever French thief, later an honest private detective and Father Brown's friend. Aristide Valentin: head of the Paris police, a sceptical, logical Frenchman. Hampstead Heath: where the thief is caught. Harwich: the port where Valentin lands. Westminster: where the real cross is posted. The Blue Cross: a silver cross set with sapphires, carried from Essex. Vernon Hotel: a very grand small hotel in Belgravia, London, where the Twelve True Fishermen dine. Mr Lever: its owner. Mr Audley: the club's chairman. The Duke of Chester: its young vice-president. Colonel Pound: a stiff, silent member. Ruby Adams: a girl near Putney. Colonel Adams: her silent father. Sir Leopold Fischer: her rich godfather. John Crook: a young journalist and Socialist who loves Ruby. James Blount: the cheerful uncle from Canada. Florian: the French acrobat and actor who plays the policeman. The Flying Stars: three huge African diamonds. Boxing Day: the day after Christmas. John Turnbull Angus: a young Scottish artist. Laura Hope: a girl in a sweet shop in Camden Town. Isidore Smythe: a small, clever inventor of clockwork servants, now a millionaire. James Welkin: a tall man with a squint, who becomes a postman. Himylaya Mansions: the tall block of flats. Lucknow Mansions: where Flambeau lives. Ludbury: Laura's home town. Bohun Beacon: a hilltop village. Colonel Norman Bohun: a wild, wealthy colonel. Wilfred Bohun: his devout priest brother. Simeon Barnes: the huge blacksmith. Gibbs: the village cobbler. Mad Joe: a simple-minded village lad. Greenford: the nearby town. General Sir Arthur St Clare: a famous English general whose tomb is a national shrine. Olivier: the noble Brazilian leader. Captain Keith: St Clare's future son-in-law. Colonel Clancy: the Irish colonel. Major Murray: a stern officer from Ulster. Espado: a Brazilian spy called the Vulture. Black River: the battle. Belfast: where Murray is buried. Voice and tone: dry, witty and gently ironic; murders and deaths are stated plainly with no gore; Brown is humble and quiet, and every riddle has a simple answer.

beats.scene: A detective in a light suit steps off a boat at Harwich
beats.summary: In The Blue Cross, Valentin of the Paris police lands in England to catch the thief Flambeau.

beats.scene: A short priest with brown paper parcels drops his umbrella on a train
beats.summary: On the train Valentin finds nobody tall enough to be Flambeau, only a short Essex priest with a silver cross in a parcel.

beats.scene: Valentin spits out his coffee in a quiet restaurant with striped blinds
beats.summary: With no clue, Valentin follows the odd; in a restaurant the salt and sugar are swapped and two clergymen have thrown soup at the wall.

beats.scene: A red-faced greengrocer points up the road beside swapped fruit labels
beats.summary: At a greengrocer's the labels for nuts and oranges are swapped and a clergyman has spilled the apples.

beats.scene: Valentin and two policemen ride on top of a yellow bus
beats.summary: A policeman says the clergymen took a bus to Hampstead, and at a restaurant Valentin finds a window that a clergyman paid for and then smashed.

beats.scene: A woman in a sweet shop shows Valentin the way to the Heath
beats.summary: In a sweet shop a woman says a clergyman asked her to post a lost parcel to Westminster, and that the two men walked on to Hampstead Heath.

beats.scene: Two priests sit on an old bench on Hampstead Heath at sunset
beats.summary: On the Heath the detectives creep close and hear two priests speak of reason and heaven, until the tall one says he is Flambeau and demands the cross.

beats.scene: Flambeau tears open a brown paper parcel and finds only paper and lead
beats.summary: Flambeau boasts that he swapped the parcels, but Brown had swapped them back and left the real cross to be posted; the parcel holds only paper and lead.

beats.scene: Valentin and two policemen step out from behind the trees
beats.summary: Brown explains how he tested Flambeau and left a trail; he knew Flambeau was no priest because he attacked reason; Valentin arrests him and bows to Brown.

beats.scene: Twelve gentlemen in green coats sit at a long table above a garden
beats.summary: In The Queer Feet, the Twelve True Fishermen hold their yearly dinner at the Vernon Hotel, where twelve silver fish knives and forks set with pearls are laid out.

beats.scene: Father Brown writes at a small table in a dim room beside the cloakroom
beats.summary: Brown has come to the hotel to hear a dying waiter, and the owner Mr Lever lets him write a note in a small room by the cloakroom.

beats.scene: Father Brown listens, head on one side, to footsteps in the passage
beats.summary: While writing, Brown hears odd footsteps in the passage: a swift light run, then a slow heavy stamp, again and again, always with the same creak.

beats.scene: Father Brown frowns in the dark, imagining feet dancing along a corridor
beats.summary: Brown decides the slow steps belong to an idle gentleman, while the swift, soft steps remind him of something he cannot remember.

beats.scene: A tall man in evening dress asks for his coat at the cloakroom counter
beats.summary: A tall, elegant man comes to the cloakroom, asks for his hat and coat and throws down half a sovereign; Brown says he must have silver in his pocket.

beats.scene: The tall man leaps over the counter but the small priest stands firm
beats.summary: The stranger vaults the counter and seizes the priest, who says he is a priest ready to hear Flambeau's confession; the thief collapses into a chair.

beats.scene: A waiter stops dead as twelve men in green coats look up
beats.summary: At dinner the silver is gone; Mr Lever says he never sent the waiter who took the plates, and the guests realise a thief has played a waiter.

beats.scene: Father Brown lays shining silver forks on the cloakroom counter
beats.summary: Brown produces the silver beside a burst window and explains that the thief played both a gentleman and a waiter, because their evening dress is the same; the club decides to wear green coats.

beats.scene: A girl in furs feeds birds while a young man sits on a wall
beats.summary: In The Flying Stars, on Boxing Day near Putney, Ruby Adams feeds the birds when the young journalist John Crook jumps down from the wall.

beats.scene: A green car stops and an old man is unwrapped from his furs
beats.summary: Ruby's rich godfather, Sir Leopold Fischer, arrives in a green car; Colonel Adams, James Blount and Father Brown welcome him.

beats.scene: Three huge diamonds blaze in an orange velvet case before a firelit hall
beats.summary: Sir Leopold shows his Christmas gift for Ruby, three huge African diamonds called the Flying Stars because they have been stolen so often.

beats.scene: A messenger hands a letter to James Blount at the open front door
beats.summary: A messenger brings Blount a letter from his old friend Florian, a famous French actor; Blount proposes a Christmas pantomime and gives out the parts.

beats.scene: Father Brown wears a paper donkey's head while Blount holds a paper tail
beats.summary: The cast dress up in silver paper, flour and paste jewels; Blount puts a paper donkey's head on Brown and pretends to pin a tail on Sir Leopold's coat.

beats.scene: A glittering harlequin dances over a limp policeman on a stage in a hall
beats.summary: In the pantomime the harlequin knocks down Florian the policeman and tosses him about like a sack; Sir Leopold searches his pockets and storms out.

beats.scene: A pantaloon in white paint faces an angry old man in a study
beats.summary: Sir Leopold says the diamonds have vanished; Brown turns out his pockets and says a man who steals diamonds does not talk Socialism, so they should look for the man they do not know.

beats.scene: Father Brown bends over the motionless policeman on the curtained stage
beats.summary: The policeman is still lying on the stage; Brown asks when Mrs Adams died, learns that Blount arrived a week too late, and finds the policeman drugged with chloroform.

beats.scene: A glittering silver figure hangs in a moonlit tree above a small priest
beats.summary: Brown finds Flambeau in the tree, praises the plot, begs him to give back the stones and give up crime; the diamonds fall and Flambeau vanishes, his last crime.

beats.scene: A red-haired young man proposes to a girl in a sweet shop
beats.summary: In The Invisible Man, the artist John Turnbull Angus orders a bun and coffee in a Camden Town sweet shop and asks Laura Hope, who serves him, to marry him.

beats.scene: Laura Hope tells her story at a table in the shop
beats.summary: Laura tells Angus of two men who once wanted to marry her at Ludbury: Isidore Smythe, now a rich inventor, and James Welkin, a tall man with a squint, whom she fears.

beats.scene: A small man in a top hat points at a paper strip
beats.summary: Smythe arrives in a small car and shows a strip of paper on the window saying that if Laura marries him he will die; he has had five threatening letters at his flat.

beats.scene: A scrap of paper in red ink lies among rows of headless clockwork servants
beats.summary: Angus drives with Smythe to Himylaya Mansions and finds a new note in red ink threatening Smythe; he goes to fetch the detective Flambeau.

beats.scene: Angus pays four men, including a chestnut seller, to watch the door
beats.summary: Angus sets four men to watch the building, then goes to Flambeau's flat, where he finds him with Father Brown, and it begins to snow.

beats.scene: Grey footprints cross the snowy doorway between the legs of a gold-braided doorman
beats.summary: The four watchers swear nobody went in, but Brown shows footprints in the new snow; upstairs there is a stain on the floor but Smythe has gone.

beats.scene: A policeman runs up the road in the snow with news for Father Brown
beats.summary: The policeman Brown had sent away runs back to say that Smythe's body has been found in the canal below, killed by a stab; Brown asks if a light brown sack was found.

beats.scene: Father Brown walks downhill in the snow, explaining, with two men beside him
beats.summary: Brown explains that people answer what you mean, not what you ask, so a man did go in and out unnoticed, because the letters had to be carried to Laura by someone.

beats.scene: Father Brown puts a hand on a postman's shoulder in the snowy street
beats.summary: Brown stops a passing postman, who turns with a terrible squint: Welkin, the murderer, who carried the body away in his mail bag; Angus returns to Laura; Brown walks the hills with the murderer.

beats.scene: Two brothers meet in a village street at dawn
beats.summary: In The Hammer of God, the brothers Norman and Wilfred Bohun meet at dawn in Bohun Beacon; Norman wears a steel-lined hat, and Wilfred warns him about the huge blacksmith.

beats.scene: A man in evening dress lies among hammers in a smithy yard
beats.summary: Later Wilfred is fetched to the smithy yard, where the colonel lies dead from a single blow; the cobbler and doctor say only the blacksmith could have struck it.

beats.scene: A small priest studies a small hammer as a huge man arrives
beats.summary: Brown wonders why so big a man would use so small a hammer; the blacksmith is arrested, but two friends prove he spent the night at a prayer meeting in Greenford.

beats.scene: A doctor whispers to a curate while a red-haired woman weeps on a bench
beats.summary: The doctor suspects the blacksmith's wife, but Brown says no woman could strike such a blow; Wilfred blames Mad Joe, but Brown says that theory is not true.

beats.scene: The blacksmith faces the inspector in his yard and speaks of a thunderbolt
beats.summary: The blacksmith says no thing of flesh held the hammer; Brown gives the doctor two hints: it is a matter of physical science, and a flying hammer is nearest the truth.

beats.scene: Two priests stand on a high stone balcony of a church tower
beats.summary: Brown takes Wilfred up the tower and tells of a man who prayed in high places until he fancied himself God; when Wilfred puts a leg over the wall, Brown pulls him back.

beats.scene: Wilfred Bohun speaks to the inspector at the gate of the smithy yard
beats.summary: Brown says he knows what Wilfred did and will tell no one, leaving the next step to him; Wilfred goes down and tells the inspector he killed his brother.

beats.scene: Two men in black stand in a frozen churchyard before a great metal tomb
beats.summary: In The Sign of the Broken Sword, Brown and Flambeau visit the tomb of General St Clare on a frozen night, and Brown asks where a wise man hides a leaf.

beats.scene: Brown talks to Flambeau as they walk along a frozen forest road
beats.summary: Brown tells what everyone knows: St Clare attacked the Brazilian leader Olivier with a small force, was captured, and was found hanged with his broken sword round his neck.

beats.scene: Brown reads a printed page in the moonlight on a forest road
beats.summary: Brown gives two clues: Captain Keith's book says St Clare was no fool and Olivier no brute, and Olivier's dispatch praises the English last stand.

beats.scene: Flambeau strides ahead through the dark woods, guessing aloud
beats.summary: Flambeau guesses that the general, fearing madness in his family, wished to die in battle and killed himself in despair; Brown says it is a clean story, and the truth is worse.

beats.scene: A general on a white horse talks with a tall major
beats.summary: Brown gives the last clues: Colonel Clancy's dying curse about the sword, and a soldier's diary from the spy Espado's papers, telling how the general spoke with Major Murray and then ordered the attack.

beats.scene: Brown points to a frozen puddle shining under the moon as Flambeau listens
beats.summary: Brown says the other half of the sword lies in Major Murray's grave in Belfast; a wise man with no forest grows one, and to hide a body a man may make a field of dead.

beats.scene: English soldiers on a hot hill turn their faces towards their white-haired general
beats.summary: Brown believes St Clare sold secrets for money, killed Murray when he found out, sent his men into a hopeless battle to hide the body, and was hanged by his own soldiers.

beats.scene: Two men stand at an inn door under a sign of a broken sword
beats.summary: They reach an inn called The Sign of the Broken Sword; Brown decides to keep the secret because no innocent person is blamed, and they go in for a warm drink.

A1A2: In The Blue Cross, Valentin of the Paris police comes to England to catch Flambeau.
On the train, Valentin sees a short priest with many brown paper parcels.
In a restaurant, Valentin finds salt in the sugar and soup on the wall.
At a fruit shop, the signs for nuts and oranges are in the wrong places.
Valentin and two policemen ride on a bus after the two priests.
A shop woman says a priest left a parcel, and she posted it.
On the Heath, the tall priest says, “I am Flambeau.”
Flambeau laughs and says he has the cross, but he has not.
Father Brown says he knew Flambeau was not a priest because he attacked reason.
In The Queer Feet, a rich club has a dinner at a grand hotel.
Father Brown is writing in a small room by the hotel's coat room.
Father Brown hears strange steps: first fast, then slow, then fast again.
He thinks the slow steps are a rich man's, but the fast ones puzzle him.
A tall man asks for his coat and gives Brown a gold coin.
Brown says he is a priest, and the thief sits down, shocked.
At dinner, the silver fish knives and forks are suddenly missing.
The thief dressed as a gentleman and as a waiter, says Brown.
In The Flying Stars, Ruby feeds the birds on the day after Christmas.
Ruby's rich godfather arrives in a green car, wrapped in furs.
Sir Leopold shows three huge diamonds, called the Flying Stars.
A letter says a French actor will visit, so they plan a play.
They make funny clothes from paper, and Brown wears a donkey's head.
The man in silver hits the policeman, and everyone laughs loudly.
Brown says the thief is not Crook but the man they do not know.
The policeman on the stage is not an actor, but a real policeman.
In the end, Flambeau gives back the diamonds and stops stealing.
In The Invisible Man, Angus asks Laura to marry him in a shop.
Laura says two men once wanted to marry her, and both left.
A strip of paper on the window threatens Smythe with death.
In Smythe's hall, there is a new threat written in red ink.
Angus asks four men to watch the door of the building.
Four men say nobody went in, but there are footprints in the snow.
The policeman runs back and says Smythe is dead in the canal.
Brown says the men saw a visitor, but did not notice him.
The man who brings the letters is Welkin, and he killed Smythe.
In The Hammer of God, two very different brothers meet at dawn.
Later, the colonel is found dead in the blacksmith's yard.
The blacksmith was far away all night, so he is not the killer.
Wilfred says the village lad did it, but Brown says no.
The blacksmith thinks God sent the blow, but Brown disagrees.
Brown pulls Wilfred back from the edge of the high tower.
At last, Wilfred goes to the inspector and tells the truth.
In The Sign of the Broken Sword, two men visit a great tomb.
The great general was captured in Brazil and later found hanged.
An officer wrote that St Clare was no fool, but said no more.
Flambeau thinks the general was mad, but Brown says it was worse.
A soldier's diary tells of a talk by the river before the attack.
Brown says the missing piece of sword lies in a grave in Belfast.
The general killed Murray, and later his own men hanged him.
Brown will keep the secret, and the two men go into the inn.
B1B2: In The Blue Cross, Aristide Valentin, head of the Paris police, steps off a boat at Harwich and takes the train to London. He has come to arrest Flambeau, a famous thief who is believed to be hiding somewhere in the city.

Flambeau is over six feet tall, so Valentin looks only for tall people, and he finds none. The only unusual traveller is a short priest from Essex, who drops his umbrella and says that one parcel holds silver with blue stones.

Valentin has no clue, so he follows anything strange, and in a quiet restaurant he finds salt in the sugar bowl. The waiter blames two clergymen, who also threw their soup at the wall before they left.

Round the corner, a shop has put the sign for oranges on the nuts and the sign for nuts on the oranges. The angry owner says that a clergyman spilled his apples and walked off up the road with a friend.

A policeman says the clergymen took a bus to Hampstead, so Valentin takes two officers and follows them on top of the bus. At a restaurant on the road, the waiter says a clergyman paid for a window and then smashed it with his umbrella.

Valentin buys some sweets in a small shop and learns that a clergyman came back to ask about a lost parcel. The woman has already posted it to an address in Westminster, and the two clergymen have gone towards Hampstead Heath.

Valentin and the policemen creep through the grass until they can hear the two priests talking quietly about reason and heaven. Then the taller man suddenly says, “Give me that sapphire cross, for I am Flambeau.”

Flambeau laughs and says he has already swapped the parcels, so the little priest holds only a copy. Father Brown calmly answers that he saw the swap, changed the parcels back, and left the true cross behind to be posted away.

Father Brown explains that he swapped the salt and sugar and broke the window to leave a trail for the police. He knew the tall man was no priest, because he attacked reason, and now Valentin steps out and arrests him.

In The Queer Feet, a club called the Twelve True Fishermen holds its yearly dinner at the Vernon Hotel, a very grand hotel. At the fish course, the members use twelve silver knives and forks, each made like a fish and set with a pearl.

That evening Father Brown has been called to the hotel to help a waiter who is seriously ill upstairs. The owner, Mr Lever, does not want a shabby priest to be seen, so he puts him in a small room by the cloakroom.

As he writes, Father Brown notices a strange pattern of footsteps in the passage outside. First he hears quick, light steps, then a slow, heavy walk, and then the quick steps again, always with the same creak.

Father Brown decides that the slow, careless steps belong to a gentleman who has never worked for his living. The quick, soft steps remind him of something he has seen before, but he cannot remember what.

Father Brown steps into the empty cloakroom, where a tall, elegant man in evening dress asks for his hat and coat. The man has no silver, he says, and tosses down a gold coin, but Brown says he is sure that his pocket holds some.

The stranger jumps over the counter and grabs the little priest by the collar. Father Brown calmly says that he is a priest and is ready to hear Flambeau's confession, and the thief falls into a chair.

In the dining room, the club members find that their silver fish knives and forks have vanished from the table. The owner says he never sent the waiter who took the plates, and the guests guess that a thief has pretended to be a waiter.

Father Brown lays the silver on the counter and explains that one man played both a gentleman and a waiter. Since a gentleman's evening dress looks just like a waiter's, the club decides to wear green coats from that night on.

In The Flying Stars, a girl named Ruby Adams goes into her garden near Putney on Boxing Day to feed the birds. A young journalist called John Crook, who was born next door, jumps down from the wall beside her.

Ruby's godfather, a rich old financier called Sir Leopold Fischer, arrives in a green car, wrapped up in rugs and furs. Her father Colonel Adams, her uncle James Blount, and Father Brown, the local priest, come out to welcome him.

In the hall, Sir Leopold takes a black case from his coat and opens it to show three huge diamonds on orange velvet. They are called the Flying Stars, he says, because they have been stolen so many times.

A messenger brings James Blount a letter from an old friend, Florian, a famous French acrobat and actor, who will visit that night. Blount suggests a Christmas pantomime, with himself as harlequin, Crook as clown, and Florian dressed as a policeman.

The harlequin is dressed in silver paper and false jewels, and the clown and the pantaloon are powdered with flour. Blount puts a paper donkey's head on Father Brown, who bears it patiently, and he pretends to pin a tail on Sir Leopold's coat.

Florian bursts in dressed as a policeman, and the harlequin knocks him down and swings him about like a sack. The audience roars with laughter, but Sir Leopold suddenly rises, searches his pockets, and storms out of the room.

In the study, Sir Leopold cries that his diamonds have vanished, and he hints that Crook or Father Brown has taken them. Brown turns out his pockets and says they should look instead at the one man nobody knows, the actor who plays the policeman.

The colonel says the policeman has been lying on the stage through six curtain calls, and Father Brown suddenly asks when Mrs Adams died. Then he rushes to the stage, finds the man drugged with chloroform, and cries that he is a real policeman.

Father Brown finds Flambeau, who has played Blount the farmer and the harlequin, glittering in a tree in the moonlight. He begs him to give up crime, and three diamonds fall to the grass before the tree is empty.

In The Invisible Man, a young Scottish artist called John Turnbull Angus goes into a sweet shop in Camden Town. He orders a bun and a coffee, and then he asks the girl who serves him, Laura Hope, to marry him.

Laura says that two men in her old village once wanted to marry her, the small Isidore Smythe and the tall, squinting James Welkin. She had said she would marry only a man who had made his own way, so both went away to seek their fortunes.

Smythe drives up and points to a strip of paper on the window, which says, “If you marry Smythe, he will die.” He has had five threatening letters at his flat, he says, and nobody has seen who left them.

Angus goes with Smythe to his flat at the top of Himylaya Mansions, where rows of headless clockwork servants stand in the hall. On the floor lies a new note in red ink that says, “If you have been to see her today, I shall kill you.”

Before he leaves, Angus asks four men to watch the building: a porter, a doorman, a policeman and a man selling chestnuts. Then he goes to the flat of his friend Flambeau, an honest detective, who is sitting with a small priest, Father Brown.

All four watchers swear that nobody has gone into the building, but Father Brown points to a line of grey footprints in the new snow. Angus and Flambeau rush upstairs and find a red stain on the floor, but Smythe has disappeared.

Father Brown had quietly sent the policeman down the road, and now the man comes running back, out of breath. Smythe's body has been found in the canal below the mansions, he says, and the little man has been stabbed.

Father Brown explains that people answer what you mean, not what you say, so the watchers meant that nobody suspicious went in. A man did go in and out, but nobody noticed him, because he was invisible only in their minds.

Father Brown puts his hand on the shoulder of a passing postman, who turns round with a terrible squint. It is Welkin, who killed Smythe and carried the body away in his mail bag, unnoticed because he was only a postman.

In The Hammer of God, two brothers meet at dawn in a hilltop village, one a wild colonel and the other a priest. The colonel wears a green hat lined with steel, and the priest warns him to fear the huge blacksmith.

Soon after, a cobbler fetches Wilfred from the church, because his brother lies dead in the smithy yard. Everyone agrees that only one man in the district is strong enough to have struck such a blow, and that man is the blacksmith.

Father Brown notices that the hammer used was one of the smallest, and he wonders why a strong man would choose it. The inspector arrests the blacksmith, but two respectable men prove that he spent the whole night at a prayer meeting miles away.

The doctor thinks a woman used the small hammer, but Father Brown says no woman could have struck such a blow. Wilfred then blames Mad Joe, a simple-minded village lad, but Brown says gently that this theory, though clever, is not true.

Barnes says that no creature of flesh held the hammer, and he believes that God himself struck down the colonel. Father Brown says the blow was a matter of science, and that a flying hammer is nearer the truth than it sounds.
Father Brown talks of a man who prayed in high places and began to feel like God. When Wilfred puts a leg over the wall of the tower, Brown pulls him back by the collar.

Father Brown says he knows what Wilfred did, but he will keep it secret and leave the next step to him. Wilfred walks down to the smithy and tells the inspector, “I wish to give myself up, for I have killed my brother.”
In The Sign of the Broken Sword, Father Brown and Flambeau stand at night before the tomb of a famous general. Father Brown asks where a wise man hides a leaf, and Flambeau answers, “In the forest.”

Everyone knows that St Clare, a brave and careful general, attacked the Brazilian leader Olivier at the Black River with a very small army. He was captured, and everyone believes that Olivier then hanged him, with his broken sword hung round his neck.

Captain Keith, an officer at the battle, wrote that St Clare was no fool and Olivier no brute, but he would say no more. Olivier's report praises the last stand of the English, with the general bareheaded on horseback holding a broken sword.

Flambeau guesses that St Clare feared madness in his family, wished to die in battle, and killed himself when he was only captured. Father Brown calls it a clean and honest story, and he says sadly that the truth is much worse.

The last clues are a dying colonel's angry words about the sword and a soldier's diary found among a Brazilian official's papers. It describes how the general rode off with Major Murray, then galloped back and ordered the attack, his sword still whole.
Father Brown says that the other half of the sword lies in Major Murray's grave in Belfast, under a monument to a hero. To hide a dead body, he adds, a man might make a whole battlefield of them.

Father Brown believes that St Clare, short of money, sold secrets to the enemy, and killed Major Murray when he found out. To hide the crime he sent his men into a hopeless battle, and later his own men, who had guessed the truth, hanged him.

At last they reach an inn whose sign shows a broken sword, a reminder of how famous the general has become. Father Brown decides to keep the secret, since no innocent man is blamed, and the two friends go inside to get warm.
C1C2: On a bright morning in the story called The Blue Cross, the boat touched Harwich, and among the crowd walked Aristide Valentin, the head of the Paris police and the most famous detective in Europe. Beneath his holiday clothes he carried a loaded revolver and a police card, though nothing in his face gave him away. He had crossed the sea to make the greatest arrest of the century, for Flambeau, the cleverest thief alive, was known to be somewhere in England.

There was one thing that Flambeau, with all his gift for disguise, could never hide, and that was his enormous height. Valentin therefore studied every traveller on the journey to London and found nobody tall enough, so his attention rested at last on a round-faced little priest from Essex, who kept dropping his shabby umbrella. Cheerfully, the priest explained to the whole carriage that one of his brown paper parcels held a silver cross set with blue stones.

With no clue to guide him, Valentin trusted the odd instead of the sensible, and he walked into a quiet restaurant simply because its steps and striped blinds appealed to him. There he put sugar in his coffee, tasted salt, and discovered that the salt cellars were full of sugar. The waiter, horrified, remembered that two clergymen had thrown their soup against the wall before they left, and Valentin sprang to his feet.

Hurrying round the corner, Valentin caught sight of a greengrocer's shop where a card marked tangerines lay on a heap of nuts and a card marked Brazil nuts lay on a heap of oranges. He recognised the same strange humour that had changed the salt and the sugar, and he asked the red-faced owner what he knew of two clergymen, one tall and one short. The man answered angrily that one of them had spilled his apples across the road, and that both had gone up the second street on the left.

A policeman remembered two clergymen boarding a yellow omnibus for Hampstead, so Valentin summoned an inspector and a plain-clothes man and climbed up after them, though he could not explain what he was hoping to find. Somewhere in the long northern suburbs he leapt up and stopped the bus, for he had seen a restaurant window with a great black star smashed into the glass. Inside, the waiter told him that a clergyman had paid far too much for his lunch, announced that the extra would pay for a window, and broken the pane with his umbrella.

In a gaudy little sweet shop Valentin bought thirteen chocolate cigars with great care, preparing some excuse for his questions, but the shopwoman saw the inspector's blue uniform in the doorway and spoke at once. A clergyman, she said, had run back to ask whether he had left a parcel, and when she found nothing he had given her an address in Westminster and a shilling in case it turned up. Afterwards she had found a brown paper parcel after all and posted it to him, so Valentin hurried out and ran for the open heath.

Using every trick of the deer-stalker, Valentin and his two policemen crawled behind trees until they were close enough to hear the priests, who were discussing reason and the heavens as gravely as any pair of scholars in a cloister. Valentin was beginning to fear that he had made a fool of himself when the tall priest, without changing his bowed head or his gentle voice, asked the other to hand over his sapphire cross. “Yes, I am Flambeau,” he added quietly, “and we are all alone here, so you had better do as I say.”

Flambeau threw back his head and laughed, for he believed that he had already exchanged the real parcel for a duplicate of brown paper and lead, and that the silly little priest was guarding nothing. Father Brown, rubbing his hair in apologetic bewilderment, replied that he had heard of that old trick before and had suspected the tall stranger from the very first meeting. He had watched the exchange, switched the parcels back again, and then deliberately left the true one behind in the sweet shop, so that it would be posted safely to a friend in Westminster.

Father Brown explained that he had swapped the salt and the sugar and changed the bill, because a man who says nothing at such moments has a reason for not being noticed. Since Flambeau would leave no tracks, the little priest had made some himself, with a splashed wall, spilled apples and a broken window, and now the policemen walked out from under the trees. He had known the stranger was no clergyman because he had attacked reason, which is bad theology, and as Flambeau swept Valentin a splendid bow, the Frenchman replied that they should both bow to their master.

Members of the club called the Twelve True Fishermen wear green evening coats instead of black, and the reason is the story of The Queer Feet. Their yearly dinner is held at the Vernon Hotel, a small, silent and tremendously exclusive place that makes its fortune by turning customers away. For the great dinner the Fishermen lay out their treasure, twelve knives and forks of silver wrought in the shape of fish, each with a single large pearl set in the handle.

That afternoon a waiter at the hotel had been struck down by a stroke, and his employer, Mr Lever, had unwillingly agreed to send for the nearest Catholic priest. Father Brown heard the man's confession, and since it required him to write down a message, he asked for a room and paper. Mr Lever, who dreaded anything that might disturb his famous guests, shut the shabby little priest in a small private room between the glass office and the cloakroom, where he began to write.

As he wrote the last paragraphs of his document, Father Brown caught himself writing to the rhythm of a noise outside, and he realised that it was only footsteps passing in the corridor. Yet the footsteps were very odd, for a long rush of swift, light little steps would suddenly change into a slow, swinging stamp, and then the swift steps would begin again. Because there were no other boots in the passage and these had a small but unmistakable creak, he was certain that one man was making both sounds.

Sitting in the gathering dark, Father Brown followed the sounds with his finger on the edge of the table, like a man learning a tune on the piano, and began to wonder what they meant. The slow, springy tread, with its careless emphasis, could belong only to a well-fed gentleman of western Europe who had never worked for his living. The swift, noiseless step reminded him of something he had met before but could not name, and when it came again, bounding like a panther, he smelt evil as a dog smells rats.

Groping through a forest of overcoats, Father Brown reached the half-door of the cloakroom, where an elegant stranger in plain evening dress stood in the light of the corridor, his black coat bulging oddly. The man tossed down a ticket, asked briskly for his hat and coat because he had to go away at once, and flung half a sovereign on the counter instead of silver. Father Brown, who had at that instant understood everything, answered politely that he thought the gentleman had some silver in his pocket, since silver is sometimes more valuable than gold.

The stranger looked at him curiously, then glanced up the passage towards the entrance and at the window behind the priest's head, and vaulted over the counter as lightly as an acrobat. He seized Father Brown by the collar, but the little priest only looked up at him without the slightest fear. “I am a priest, Monsieur Flambeau,” said Brown, “and I am ready to hear your confession,” and the great thief staggered back into a chair, gasping.

The dinner was proceeding in placid splendour when a waiter stopped dead, hurried away to fetch another waiter, and then another, until the proprietor himself came running with a sickly yellow face. Their fish plates, he panted, had been cleared away with the knives and forks still on them by a waiter whom he had never sent, and the young duke swore that he had counted fifteen waiters. One of the fifteen, Mr Lever reminded them, lay ill upstairs, so Colonel Pound, who rarely spoke, rose at once and declared that the extra man had been a thief.

Behind him, the window of the little room was burst open, as if someone had passed violently through it, but on the counter Father Brown calmly laid out a dozen shining knives and forks. He explained that the clever crime rested on one plain fact, that a gentleman's evening dress is the same as a waiter's, so the thief had played both parts and nobody had suspected either. The club laughed with relief, and Colonel Pound proposed that from then on the members should wear green coats, since one never knows what mistakes may arise when one looks so like a waiter.

The story of The Flying Stars begins on Boxing Day in a comfortable house near Putney, where a pretty girl called Ruby Adams came out in her brown furs to scatter bread for the birds. High on the garden wall sat a tall, restless young man in a red tie, John Crook, who leapt to the ground and cheerfully remarked that he was meant to be a burglar. He was a journalist with fierce opinions and a fondness for Ruby, and he had been born in the house on the other side of the wall.

A motor horn sounded three times, and a pale green car swept up to the door, from which a chauffeur and a manservant unpacked Sir Leopold Fischer, a rich financier, from rugs, furs and scarves. He was Ruby's godfather, and Colonel Adams, her tall and silent father, came out to greet him, together with her uncle James Blount, a cheerful farmer lately arrived from Canada, and the small priest Father Brown. John Crook, who had written fierce articles against rich men like Sir Leopold, watched the whole performance with a grim smile.

Beside the great hall fire, Sir Leopold drew a black oval case from his coat and held it out with childlike pride, and it flew open as if a crystal fountain had spurted. In a nest of orange velvet lay three white diamonds so brilliant that they seemed to set the air on fire, and Ruby cried out in wonder while her father murmured his thanks. They were the African stones known as the Flying Stars, the old man explained, because they had been stolen so often, and he slipped them back into his coat tails.

A dusty messenger knocked at the door with a letter for Mr Blount, who read it with surprise and explained that his old friend Florian, the famous French acrobat and comic actor, was coming that very night. Blount, who was like a schoolboy in his excitement, cried that they must all put on an old English pantomime in the hall, with Crook as the clown, himself as harlequin, Ruby as columbine, and the colonel as pantaloon. He telephoned Florian to bring a policeman's costume, and the whole house plunged into preparing a performance within a few hours.

The preparations were wild and cheerful, for youth and happiness filled the house that night, and everyone hurried about with paper, paint and string. The harlequin was covered in silver paper and glittering paste jewels, the clown and pantaloon whitened their faces with the cook's flour, and Ruby made a skirt of what looked suspiciously like the drawing-room lamp-shade. Blount, behaving like a schoolboy, fixed a paper donkey's head on Father Brown, who bore it patiently, and pretended to pin a tail to the coat of Sir Leopold, who frowned.

The pantomime was chaotic but not contemptible, and Crook, the clown, was the author, the prompter and the orchestra all at once, throwing himself at the piano to bang out absurd tunes. The climax came when the doors flew open on the moonlit garden and the famous Florian appeared as a policeman, whereupon the harlequin struck him on the helmet and swung him about like a sack. Behind his dancing victim the glittering harlequin retreated slowly into the garden, and in the front row Father Brown noticed that Sir Leopold had jumped up, thrust his hands into his pockets, and rushed from the room.

In his study, still in his pantaloon's paint, Colonel Adams sadly explained that Sir Leopold's diamonds had vanished from his coat pocket, and that his friend was loudly blaming the young Socialist. Father Brown, who had been sitting directly behind the financier, turned out his own pockets, which held seven and sixpence, a return ticket, a small silver cross, a prayer book and a stick of chocolate. He pointed out that men who mean to steal diamonds do not make speeches about Socialism, and that they ought rather to look for the one man they did not know, the French actor playing the policeman.

The colonel came back to report that the policeman was still lying on the stage and that the curtain had gone up and down six times. Father Brown stared in blank dismay and asked when the colonel's wife had died, and he learned that she had died two months before and that her brother James had arrived from Canada a week too late. The little priest bounded like a shot rabbit, ran to the stage, bent over the motionless figure, and declared that the man had been drugged with chloroform and was a real policeman.

In the moonlit garden a figure sparkling from head to foot was climbing among the treetops, and beneath it stood Father Brown, who told Flambeau that this was the cleverest plot he had ever made. Then he begged him to return the stones and give up crime, warning him that the road of evil goes down and down. Three flashing diamonds dropped to the turf, and when the small man looked up again the silver bird had flown, ending what Flambeau called his most beautiful crime and also his last.

In the cool blue twilight of Camden Town, the corner sweet shop glowed like a firework, and a tall, red-haired young artist named John Turnbull Angus stood staring through its window at the huge white wedding cake. Walking through to the pastry-cook's room at the back, he ordered his usual halfpenny bun and a small black coffee, and then, just as the dark-eyed girl serving him turned away, added that he also wanted her to marry him. The girl, whose name was Laura Hope, told him that she did not allow such jokes, but she looked at him with such steady attention that it was clear she was not offended.

Laura explained that her father had owned an inn at Ludbury, where two peculiar young men used to drink, and both had offered to marry her in the same week. One was Isidore Smythe, a clever little man who made dancing dolls from banana skins, and the other was James Welkin, a tall, silent man with a terrible squint. She had then said she would marry only a self-made man, so both went away, and now Smythe was a millionaire, but it was Welkin, whose laugh she kept hearing in empty places, that frightened her.

A small motor-car shrieked up to the door, and a dapper little man with a spike of black beard, Isidore Smythe himself, stamped into the shop and asked whether Miss Hope had seen the thing on the window. Along the glass a yard and a half of gummed paper had been pasted while the people inside were having tea, and on it, in straggling letters, were the words, “If you marry Smythe, he will die.” Smythe recognised the handwriting of his old rival Welkin, who had left five threatening letters at his flat within a fortnight, though neither the porter nor anyone else could say who delivered them.

Smythe drove his guest in his small, swift car up a steep, curving hill to Himylaya Mansions, a tall tower of flats that rose above the city like a lighthouse above a green sea of slate. A hidden button opened the door of the top-floor flat, and inside, between two rows of tall, headless clockwork servants that stood like tailors' dummies, lay a scrap of paper scrawled in red ink that was still wet. “If you have been to see her today, I shall kill you,” it said, and Angus, deciding that matters had become serious, hurried out to fetch his friend Flambeau, the detective.

Before leaving, Angus took every precaution, for he paid a porter on the stairs, the doorman at the entrance, a policeman across the street and an old chestnut seller to watch the building. He then hurried to Lucknow Mansions, where Flambeau, who had long ago given up crime and become a private detective, sat among sabres and a Persian cat with a small priest called Father Brown. As Angus began to tell his tale, the first flakes of snow drifted across the window, exactly as the quiet little priest had said they would.

When the three men reached the crescent, the chestnut seller, the policeman and the doorman all swore that nobody had entered the building, but Father Brown mildly asked whether anyone had passed since the snow began to fall. Then he pointed to a stringy pattern of grey footprints running straight down the middle of the entrance, between the doorman's very legs, and Angus cried out that this was the Invisible Man. Racing upstairs, he and Flambeau found the flat as before, except that a dark stain lay where the paper had been, and although they searched every corner and cupboard, Isidore Smythe was nowhere to be found.

Angus and Flambeau came down to find the watchers repeating their stories and the policeman missing, because, as Father Brown confessed, he had sent him down the road to investigate something that seemed worth investigating. Presently the big constable came running round the corner, panting that poor Mr Smythe's body had just been found in the canal below, though the little man had never come down the stairs. He had not drowned, said the policeman, but died of a great stab over the heart, and Father Brown, to everyone's surprise, asked whether anyone had found a light brown sack.

Walking briskly down the hill as the snow thickened, Father Brown remarked with great modesty that nobody ever answers what you literally say, but only what you mean. So when the four honest men swore that no man had gone into the building, they meant no man whom they could suspect, and a man had indeed gone in and come out again without being noticed. He had guessed this from the tale itself, he added, because nobody can receive a letter in an empty street unless someone has brought it, and Welkin must have carried his rival's letters to the lady himself.

Nobody ever notices postmen, said Father Brown thoughtfully, as he laid a hand on the shoulder of an ordinary man in uniform who was bustling past under the trees. The man ducked and stumbled against the fence, and as he turned a frightened face over his shoulder, all three saw the squint of Welkin, the murderer, who had carried the body away in his mail bag. Angus went back to the girl at the shop, but Father Brown walked those snowy hills for many hours with a murderer, and what they said to each other will never be known.

The village of Bohun Beacon stood on so steep a hill that the spire of its church looked like the peak of a small mountain, and at its foot two brothers met one grey morning. Colonel Norman Bohun, tall and elderly with yellow hair, sat outside the inn in evening dress and a green hat after a night of drinking, while his brother Wilfred, a thin and devout clergyman, went to early prayers. The colonel said he would call on the blacksmith, who was away at Greenford, and when Wilfred warned him that the man was strong, Norman laughed and showed that his hat was lined with steel.

Half an hour later the village cobbler found Wilfred praying in the church gallery and led him, with unusual respect, down to the smithy yard, where his brother lay dead among the hammers. A single dreadful blow had killed him, and the doctor said that no ordinary man could have delivered it, so that the force of the blow itself seemed to clear nearly everyone in the village of suspicion. Gibbs added stubbornly that only one man could have done it, the man who had the greatest reason to, and the people turned to ask where the blacksmith Simeon Barnes might be.

A small, colourless voice remarked that the blacksmith was at that moment walking up the road, and it belonged to Father Brown, a little Catholic priest who went across to the church wall to look at the hammer. He noticed that it was one of the smallest and lightest in the smithy, and he wondered aloud why so big a man should attempt so big a blow with so little a hammer. The inspector arrested Simeon Barnes for murder, but the blacksmith replied that two men from Greenford would swear he had spent the night at his prayer mission, and when they spoke, his innocence stood solid as the church.

The doctor whispered that only a woman, lacking strength for a large hammer, would pick up a small one, and he nodded towards the blacksmith's wife, who sat sobbing on a bench. Father Brown, brushing ashes from his sleeve, said that no woman ever born could have struck such a blow. Wilfred then burst out that Mad Joe, a simple-minded village lad, must have done it in a fit of madness, and Brown told him respectfully that, though clever, his theory was not the true one.

The blacksmith, convinced that heaven itself had cleared him, declared that no thing of flesh had held that hammer, and that the force of the blow had been the force there is in earthquakes. Wilfred, shaking, murmured that he had told his brother to beware of the thunderbolt, and Father Brown led him gently away, but the doctor stopped the little priest on the steps and demanded to know his secrets. Brown gave him two hints, that the matter lay in the doctor's own province of physical science, and that the blacksmith's scornful tale of a hammer with wings was the nearest thing to the truth that day.

Father Brown asked to see the church and led the shaken curate up a winding stair to an outer gallery, from which they could see the whole plain and the smithy yard, small and square, far beneath them. Quietly he spoke of a man he had known who loved to pray in high and lonely places, until in some dizzy corner of the spire his brain turned and he fancied that he was God. Then, as Brown remarked that even a small hammer dropped from such a height would strike like a bullet, Wilfred threw one leg over the parapet, and the priest caught him by the collar.

Brown said that he could guess the greater part of it, how the priest, in a black rage, had snatched up a small hammer and rushed into the church. From a high platform, he went on, Wilfred had seen the colonel's strange green hat crawling below like a beetle, and then something had snapped in his soul, and he had let the thunderbolt fall. He would tell no one, he promised, and the next step was for Wilfred alone, who went down in silence to the inspector and said, “I wish to give myself up; I have killed my brother.”

On a night of bitter frost, with stars as bleak as splintered ice, two men in black, one enormous and one very small, climbed the steep path of a village churchyard. At the top stood the monument of General Sir Arthur St Clare, whose bronze figure lay with folded hands, a Bible at his left and a sword with a broken tip at his right. By match-light they read the words that called him hero and martyr, and Father Brown asked where a wise man hides a leaf, and Flambeau answered that he hides it in the forest.

Brown divided the tale into what everybody knows and what he knew, and the first part, he said, was short and plain and quite inadequate. The public believed that Sir Arthur St Clare, a prudent soldier, had attacked the Brazilian patriot Olivier at the Black River with a tiny force against a huge one. He had been captured and hanged on the nearest tree with his broken sword round his neck, and the mystery was that a wise man had acted like an idiot and a kind man like a fiend.

Brown then produced the first of his scraps of evidence, a passage in the memoirs of Captain Keith, an officer in the doomed regiment who afterwards married the general's daughter. Keith declared that the battle at the Black River had been one of the most brilliant actions of St Clare's life, and that Olivier had behaved with generosity, but he would say no more. The second clue was the dispatch of Olivier himself, who wrote with admiration of the last stand of that extraordinary regiment, with wounded officers picking up rifles and the general facing him bareheaded on horseback with a broken sword.

Flambeau, who had been striding ahead like a man in a walking race, suddenly slapped his thigh and said that he could tell the whole story in four minutes. The general, he said, came from a family in which madness was inherited, and wishing to hide this from his daughter, he rushed into battle hoping to die. When he won only capture and disgrace, Flambeau went on, he broke his own sword and hanged himself, but the priest answered that he wished it were true, for there are worse things than madness and despair.

Brown went on to the last pieces of evidence, the angry words of Colonel Clancy, who died complaining that the old donkey had had the end of his sword knocked off. The second was a soldier's diary found among the papers of a Brazilian official named Espado, which described how the general rode into camp on his white horse and spoke earnestly with Major Murray, a stern officer from Ulster. Walking down towards the river beside the major, the general suddenly galloped back with a face like flame and ordered an attack, having half drawn his sword and thrust it back, though the colonel afterwards saw it broken.

The sword was broken, he declared, before the battle, and the missing piece lay in a cemetery at Belfast, beneath a great marble monument to Major Murray, who was said to have fallen gloriously at the Black River. When Flambeau cried that the general had hated Murray and murdered him on the battlefield, Brown answered that his mind was still full of good and pure thoughts, for it was worse than that. Again he asked where a wise man hides a leaf, and answered himself that, with no forest, he would make one, and that a man hiding a body would make a battlefield.

St Clare, said Father Brown, who admitted he could not prove it, had led a secret life of greed, and short of money he had sold information to Brazil through the spy Espado. When Major Murray guessed the truth and told him to resign, the general killed him by the river, and then, with terrible coldness, he resolved to hide that one body beneath a hill of them. He marched hundreds of his own men to their deaths, and when Olivier set the survivors free, the soldiers who had followed the general turned their faces upon him, and it was English hands that hanged him.

Over the ridge there burst upon them the scarlet light of an English inn, and Flambeau stepped back, for its sign showed a sabre hilt and a shortened blade and read The Sign of the Broken Sword. Father Brown reminded him that the general was the god of that country, with inns, streets and statues named after him, and that his marble figures would go on inspiring proud and innocent boys for centuries. He would speak, he said, only if an innocent man were blamed in marble, but since it was only that St Clare was wrongly praised, he would be silent, and they went in for wine.
